regions.name: Canary Islands
regions.summary: Seven main islands of volcanic rock in the Atlantic, Spanish since the fifteenth century, lying off the coast of southern Morocco at the latitude of the Sahara yet cooled by the trade winds, the Canary Current and height. Phylloxera never arrived, so the vines grow on their own roots, many of them old, in volcanic ground. Lanzarote plants each vine in a pit dug through black ash behind a crescent of stone; Tenerife, with five of the islands' eleven DOs, braids its vines into long cordons in the Orotava valley. Listán Blanco, which is Palomino, and Listán Negro make most of the wine, and Malvasía carries the history: the sweet Canary that England drank in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

terroir.climate: Subtropical and oceanic at sea level, with mild winters and warm, dry summers, but no one climate fits the islands. The north-east trade winds, the alisios, blow for much of the year and pile cloud against the north-facing slopes of the high western islands, a sea of clouds that brings mist, moisture and shade; the southern slopes, in the lee, are sunny and dry. The cool Canary Current keeps the sea temperate for the latitude. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura, low and close to Africa, are arid, and the hot, dusty wind off the Sahara, the calima, can scorch vines in summer. Height is the grower's thermostat: every few hundred metres climbed buys freshness and a later harvest.
terroir.soils: Volcanic throughout, from young lava and black lapilli to older weathered basalt and ash. On Lanzarote a layer of picón, the lapilli thrown out by the eruptions of 1730 to 1736, buried the old farmland, in places metres deep; growers dig through it to plant, and on the surface it acts as a mulch, catching dew and the little rain and slowing evaporation. Tenerife's soils change from valley to valley, from loams and clays over old volcanic rock in the wetter north to pale pumice and sandy ash in the dry south. Phylloxera never reached the islands, and the import of vines is controlled to keep it out.
terroir.topography: The western islands rise steeply out of deep ocean. Teide, 3,715 metres, stands over Tenerife, and the island's vineyards run from near the coast to well above 1,000 metres in the south around Vilaflor. La Palma, El Hierro and La Gomera are steep, ravine-cut cones, and Gran Canaria a round massif. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura in the east are older, lower and flatter, with Lanzarote's volcanic fields of Timanfaya and the vine landscape of La Geria at its centre.
terroir.water: The Atlantic surrounds every vineyard, and the cool Canary Current, flowing south-west past the islands, tempers the heat of the latitude. The islands have no real rivers: moisture comes from the trade-wind cloud, from dew and from the winter rain, and Lanzarote's vines live on what the ash catches.

grapes.name: Listán Blanco
grapes.styles: Palomino under its island name and the main white grape: on volcanic soils and old own-rooted vines it gives dry whites with more salt, smoke and tension than its Andalusian reputation suggests.

grapes.name: Listán Negro
grapes.styles: The main black grape, above all on Tenerife: light to medium-bodied reds of red cherry, pepper and a smoky edge, many made young, some by carbonic maceration.

grapes.name: Malvasía Volcánica
grapes.styles: Lanzarote's own white, by the usual account a natural crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo found only in the Canaries: aromatic and saline when dry, honeyed when sweet.

grapes.name: Malvasía Aromática
grapes.styles: The old Malvasía of the sweet Canary wine, grown above all at Fuencaliente on La Palma, where it is picked late for a sweet Malvasía.

grapes.name: Negramoll
grapes.styles: The Tinta Negra of Madeira under its Canary name: pale, fragrant reds, important on La Palma and in blends with Listán Negro.

grapes.name: Marmajuelo
grapes.styles: A rare white of high acidity, also called Bermejuela, now bottled alone for dry, aromatic whites.

grapes.name: Baboso Negro
grapes.styles: A dark, aromatic red of El Hierro and Tenerife, rescued from near loss and now made alone by a handful of houses.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel, made sweet on Lanzarote, some of it fortified.

wines.note: Dry, aromatic and saline: white flowers, citrus peel and stone fruit with a smoky finish. Serve it cold with grilled fish, papas arrugadas with mojo sauce or the islands' goat's cheese.
Dry and taut, with citrus, herbs and a flinty, smoky note; old own-rooted vines in the Orotava valley and in Abona give the serious bottles, some fermented in old wood.
Light to medium-bodied, with red cherry, white pepper and smoke over fresh acidity. Serve it slightly cool with grilled meat, tuna or rabbit.
From overripe, late-picked Malvasía at Fuencaliente: honey, apricot and orange peel held by fresh acidity, the heir to the old Canary sack. Pour it with almond sweets or blue cheese.
A La Palma speciality from the north of the island, red, white or rosé kept for a few months in casks of Canary pine, with a resinous scent a guest will notice at once.

made.viticulture: Phylloxera never reached the Canaries, so vines are planted on their own roots, and many vineyards hold old vines and old varieties lost elsewhere. Each island answers its climate with its own training. On Lanzarote the grower digs a broad pit through the ash, the hoyo, down to the old soil, plants one to three vines at its base and builds a low crescent of dry stone, the zoco, on the windward side; the pits are worked wholly by hand. In the Orotava valley on Tenerife the cordón trenzado braids several long canes into a rope held off the ground on props, a system found nowhere else. Elsewhere vines grow as low bush vines, trail along the ground or, in newer plantings, run on wires. Harvest begins in high summer on the warm low ground and ends in autumn in the high vineyards. Plots are tiny, steep or scattered, labour is dear, and much vineyard was lost in the last century to bananas and tourism.
made.winemaking: Most Canary wine is made young and fresh, in steel at cool temperatures, to keep Malvasía's perfume and Listán Blanco's smoky tension. A newer generation of houses ferments with native yeasts in old wood or concrete, keeps whites on their lees and bottles single plots. Young Listán Negro reds are often made with whole bunches or by carbonic maceration for juicy, peppery fruit; others spend time in used barrels. The sweet wines are the old tradition: Malvasía left on the vine until overripe and fermented to a sweet wine, which La Palma's rules require to keep more than 45 grams of sugar per litre. Lanzarote also makes sweet Malvasía and Moscatel, some of it fortified. On La Palma the vino de tea spends up to six months, by its rules, in casks of the resinous heartwood of the Canary pine, which gives it a smell of pine and resin.

law.classification: The islands hold eleven DOs. Ten are the appellations of an island or a district: Lanzarote, La Palma, El Hierro, La Gomera and Gran Canaria, and on Tenerife five, Tacoronte-Acentejo, Valle de la Orotava, Ycoden-Daute-Isora, Valle de Güímar and Abona. Tacoronte-Acentejo, granted in 1992, was the first. Over them since 2011 the DO Islas Canarias, sold under the name Canary Wine, covers the whole archipelago: it lets a house blend fruit from more than one island or district and gives islands without a DO of their own, Fuerteventura among them, a quality label. Its use is voluntary, and it stands alongside the island DOs. The national ageing terms apply, and labels name the grape, the colour and the sweetness, seco, semidulce or dulce.
tiers: DO Islas Canarias
Since 2011, sold as Canary Wine: the whole archipelago; fruit may be blended across islands; its use is voluntary, alongside the island DOs.
Island DOs
Lanzarote, La Palma, El Hierro, La Gomera and Gran Canaria, each its own island's appellation.
Tenerife's five DOs
Tacoronte-Acentejo (1992, the first in the Canaries), Valle de la Orotava, Ycoden-Daute-Isora, Valle de Güímar and Abona.
labels: Palomino under its island name; the islands' main black grape.
Sweet; a La Palma Malvasía dulce comes from overripe, late-picked grapes.
La Palma wine kept briefly in casks of Canary pine.
The trading name of the DO Islas Canarias.

places.name: Lanzarote
places.note: The eastern island of black volcanic fields, where each vine is planted in a pit dug through ash and sheltered by a crescent of stone, for dry and sweet Malvasía Volcánica, Listán Negro and Moscatel under the DO Lanzarote.

places.name: La Geria
places.note: The vine landscape at the island's centre, thousands of hoyos ringed by zocos in the picón of the eruptions of the 1730s, worked by hand and protected as a landscape.

places.name: Tenerife
places.note: The large island under Teide, with five DOs that run from the wet north-east to the dry south; Listán Blanco and Listán Negro lead, from vineyards near the coast to well above 1,000 metres.

places.name: Tacoronte-Acentejo
places.note: The wetter north-east of the island, chiefly Listán Negro reds, many of them young; granted in 1992, the first DO of the Canaries.

places.name: Valle de la Orotava
places.note: The valley on the north coast below Teide, where the cordón trenzado braids long canes of Listán Blanco and Listán Negro into ropes held up on props.

places.name: Ycoden-Daute-Isora
places.note: The north-west around Icod de los Vinos, with vineyards from the coast to high slopes and many old varieties among the Listán.

places.name: Valle de Güímar
places.note: The east-facing valley south of Santa Cruz, whose vineyards climb high on the slopes, chiefly for whites of Listán Blanco.

places.name: Abona
places.note: The dry south, with vineyards on pumice and ash that climb above 1,000 metres around Vilaflor; whites of Listán Blanco lead.

places.name: La Palma
places.note: The steep north-western island, a DO with three subzones, Fuencaliente, Hoyo de Mazo and the north: Fuencaliente's sweet Malvasía grows on the ash of the San Antonio eruption of 1677, and the north makes vino de tea.

places.name: El Hierro
places.note: The island at the western end of the chain, where Listán Blanco, Vijariego and Baboso Negro grow on terraces and volcanic slopes under the DO El Hierro.

places.name: La Gomera
places.note: A round, ravine-cut island beside Tenerife whose DO makes chiefly whites, many of them from the local Forastera Blanca.

places.name: Gran Canaria
places.note: The round central island, with vineyards from the coast to the high interior and one DO for the whole island.

producers.name: El Grifo
producers.why: A Lanzarote house of the eighteenth century with a wine museum, known for dry and sweet Malvasía Volcánica from the island's ash.

producers.name: Bodegas Los Bermejos
producers.why: A Lanzarote house known for dry Malvasía Volcánica and for Listán Negro from the island's ash.

producers.name: Bodega Stratvs
producers.why: A La Geria estate among the pits and walls, making Malvasía Volcánica and Moscatel.

producers.name: Suertes del Marqués
producers.why: A Valle de la Orotava estate that bottles Listán Blanco and Listán Negro from old cordón trenzado vineyards plot by plot.

producers.name: Bodegas Monje
producers.why: A family house of Tacoronte-Acentejo, a long-standing name for Listán Negro reds.

producers.name: Bodegas Teneguía
producers.why: A Fuencaliente house on La Palma, a reference for sweet Malvasía from the volcanic south of the island.

exam: Place the islands: Spanish, in the Atlantic off southern Morocco, subtropical but cooled by the trade winds, the Canary Current and height.
Know why the vines are ungrafted: phylloxera never reached the islands.
Picture Lanzarote: one vine to each pit dug through black volcanic ash, sheltered by a crescent of stone.
Know Listán Blanco as Palomino and Malvasía Volcánica as Lanzarote's own white.
Know the DO Islas Canarias of 2011 over the island DOs, and that Tenerife holds five DOs.
Know the history: sweet Malvasía, called Canary or Canary sack, was shipped to England in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
Listán Negro, Negramoll and the cordón trenzado of the Orotava valley are asked from Premier Cru; the names hoyo and zoco and La Palma's vino de tea from Grand Cru.
traps: Listán Blanco is Palomino; Listán Negro is a different, black grape, so the shared name says nothing about the wine.
The Canaries are Spanish; Madeira and the Azores are Portugal's Atlantic islands.
Malvasía Volcánica is not the Malvasia of Madeira or of Italy: it is a Canary crossing.
Ungrafted here means phylloxera never arrived, not that the vines resist it.
Tenerife has five DOs, not one; the DO Islas Canarias is a label over the whole archipelago, not a sixth district of Tenerife.
Negramoll is Madeira's Tinta Negra, not the Negroamaro of Puglia.
Vino de tea is aged in pine, not oak.

cards.f: Canary Islands: where and what kind of place
cards.b: Seven main volcanic islands of Spain in the Atlantic off southern Morocco: subtropical, cooled by the trade winds, the Canary Current and height.
Phylloxera never reached the islands, so vines grow on their own roots (pie franco), and the import of vines is controlled to keep the louse out.

cards.f: Lanzarote: how a vine is planted
cards.b: In a pit dug through black volcanic ash down to the old soil, one to three vines to a pit, sheltered from the wind by a crescent of dry stone.
Lanzarote's own white, by the usual account a natural crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo: dry, aromatic and saline, or sweet.
Palomino, the Sherry grape, under its Canary name: the islands' main white, dry, taut and smoky from old own-rooted vines on volcanic soil.

cards.f: DO Islas Canarias: what and when
cards.b: Since 2011, sold as Canary Wine: one DO over the whole archipelago, allowing blends across islands, beside the ten island and district DOs.

cards.f: The Canaries' two main black grapes
cards.b: Listán Negro: the main black grape, light, peppery reds, above all on Tenerife. Negramoll: Madeira's Tinta Negra, important on La Palma.
The Valle de la Orotava on Tenerife: several long canes braided into a rope held off the ground on props, a training found nowhere else.
The hoyo is the pit dug through the picón to the old soil; the zoco is the low crescent wall of stone that shields it from the trade wind. La Geria is the landscape.

cards.f: Vino de tea: what and where
cards.b: A La Palma wine from the north of the island, kept for up to six months in casks of Canary pine heartwood, which gives a resinous scent.

questions.q: Why are most Canary Islands vines planted on their own roots rather than grafted?
opts: Grafted vines are banned by the DO rules
questions.exp: Isolation and the control of imported vines kept the phylloxera louse out, so the islands never had to graft. Rootstocks grow well in hot climates and on volcanic soils elsewhere, so neither heat nor ash explains it.

questions.q: On Lanzarote, each vine is planted at the bottom of a pit dug through which material?
questions.exp: The pits are dug through the black lapilli, the picón, that the eruptions of the 1730s spread over the island, down to the older soil beneath. Albariza is the chalk of Jerez and decomposed granite the sand of Galicia.

questions.q: Which white grape, a crossing found only in the Canaries, is the signature of Lanzarote?
questions.exp: Malvasía Volcánica is Lanzarote's own white, by the usual account a natural crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo, made dry and saline or sweet.

questions.q: Which island of the Canaries holds five DOs of its own?
questions.exp: Tenerife holds Tacoronte-Acentejo, Valle de la Orotava, Ycoden-Daute-Isora, Valle de Güímar and Abona. Gran Canaria, La Palma and Lanzarote each have one DO for the whole island.

questions.q: Which winds bring cloud and moisture to the north-facing slopes of Tenerife for much of the year?
questions.exp: The north-east trade winds, the alisios, push a sea of clouds against the northern slopes. The mistral and the tramontana blow in southern France and Catalonia, the Cape Doctor over the vineyards of the Cape in South Africa.

questions.q: Which black grape leads the red wines of Tenerife?
questions.exp: Listán Negro gives Tenerife's light, peppery reds. Tempranillo leads Rioja and Ribera del Duero, Garnacha Tintorera is the red-fleshed Alicante Bouschet, and Monastrell is the grape of Jumilla.

questions.q: What is the braided training of long canes, held up on props, used in the Valle de la Orotava called?
questions.exp: The cordón trenzado braids several canes into a long rope kept off the ground; it is found only in the Orotava valley on Tenerife.

questions.q: What is the low crescent of dry stone built on the windward side of each vine pit on Lanzarote called?
questions.exp: The zoco shelters the vine in its hoyo, the pit dug through the picón, from the trade wind. La Geria is the landscape of thousands of them.

regions.name: Txakoli and the Basque Country
regions.summary: Txakoli is the sharp, pale, faintly sparkling white of the Spanish Basque Country, grown on the green, rainy hills above the Bay of Biscay and poured from a height into tumblers in the bars of San Sebastián and Bilbao. Three DOs, one for each Basque province, make it: Getariako Txakolina in Gipuzkoa, the first, recognised in 1989; Bizkaiko Txakolina in Bizkaia, 1994; and Arabako Txakolina in Álava, 2001. Hondarrabi Zuri is the white grape and Hondarrabi Beltza the black one for the rare reds and rosés. Low in alcohol, high in acid and drunk young, it is the glass for anchovies and grilled fish.

terroir.climate: Moderate maritime, the Green Spain of the Atlantic north: mild winters, cool to warm summers and rain in every month, heaviest on the coast. The Bay of Biscay keeps both frost and heat away from the coastal vineyards, but humidity makes rot and mildew the grower's constant enemy, and ripeness never comes easily, which is why the wines are low in alcohol and high in acid. The Ayala valley in Álava, inland behind the coastal hills, has colder winters with snow, a risk of spring frost and a little less rain, and its grapes ripen further.
terroir.soils: Mostly clay and clay loam over sandstone, marl and limestone. The clays hold water and drain slowly, so vines are planted on slopes, where the rain runs off and the roots stay drier. Around Getaria the coastal hills are clay over sandstone and marl; Bizkaia's valleys mix clays with river alluvium; the Ayala valley in Álava has clay and limestone.
terroir.topography: Steep green hills and short river valleys fall to the sea, with little flat land. Getaria's vineyards climb the slopes above the town and above Zarautz and Aia, many within sight of the water and close to sea level. Bizkaia's are scattered across the province, on the coast around Bakio and in the valleys inland of Bilbao. Álava's lie inland and higher in the Ayala valley south of Bilbao, sheltered by the Sierra Salvada but still on the Atlantic side of the watershed.
terroir.water: The Bay of Biscay, the arm of the Atlantic Ocean whose Spanish shore is the Cantabrian Sea, moderates the coast, and its winds carry rain and salt air onto the vineyards of Getaria and Bakio, a salinity many find in the wine. The Nervión runs north through the Ayala valley to Bilbao, an Atlantic river that keeps Álava's txakoli on the ocean's side of the mountains.

grapes.name: Hondarrabi Zuri
grapes.styles: The white grape of nearly all txakoli, zuri meaning white in Basque: high in acid, with lemon, green apple, white flowers and a saline edge.

grapes.name: Hondarrabi Beltza
grapes.styles: Beltza means black: the grape of the rare reds and, blended with Hondarrabi Zuri, of the rosés.

grapes.name: Gros Manseng
grapes.styles: Izkiriota in Basque, the South West French grape permitted in a limited share for weight and ripeness.

grapes.name: Petit Manseng
grapes.styles: Permitted in a limited share in Bizkaia and Álava, adding body and acidity to the blend.

grapes.name: Petit Courbu
grapes.styles: Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia in the rules, another white of the French Basque side permitted in a limited share.

grapes.name: Folle Blanche
grapes.styles: Mune Mahatsa in Basque, an old white allowed in Bizkaia within a capped share of a winery's vineyard.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Permitted in small shares in the txakoli rules, as Chardonnay is, and Sauvignon Blanc in Bizkaia.

wines.note: Pale, sharp and saline, with green apple, lemon and a light prickle. Poured from a height into a wide tumbler, it goes with anchovies, sardines and the pintxos of San Sebastián's bars.
Often a shade rounder than Getaria's, with citrus, herbs and a fresh prickle; a glass for grilled fish and the oily seafood of the coast.
From the inland Ayala valley: riper, rounder and less salty than the coastal wines, still high in acid and drunk young.
Hondarrabi Beltza with Hondarrabi Zuri: pale, tart and strawberry-scented, with the same prickle; a summer aperitif.
Rare: Hondarrabi Beltza alone, light, tart and leafy, drunk cool and young in the Basque Country itself.

made.viticulture: The old Basque vineyard was trained high on pergolas, the parra, of wooden or stone posts and wire, lifting the canopy off the damp ground so that the wind could dry the bunches after rain: the same answer Galicia found at the other end of the same coast. Newer vineyards run on wires in vertical rows, easier to work and to spray, and both are seen. Slopes are chosen for drainage and sun. In wet years rot and mildew threaten from flowering to harvest and the vines are sprayed often; spring frost is the added risk inland in Álava. Holdings are small family farms, the baserri, where vines once shared the land with apple trees and pasture. Harvest comes from late September into October, when the grapes are ripe enough for a light, fresh wine, and much of it is by hand on the steeper slopes.
made.winemaking: Modern txakoli is made in temperature-controlled stainless steel tanks: a cool fermentation keeps the fresh citrus and floral aromas, and the wine is bottled young, in the months after the harvest, to be drunk within the year. Its prickle is carbon dioxide from the fermentation kept in the wine at bottling, not a second fermentation. Basque bars pour it from a height, the gesture called escanciar, into a wide tumbler, so the gas lifts and the wine freshens. Some houses keep the wine on its fine lees for a few months for texture, and a small but growing number make barrel-fermented, lees-aged or sparkling txakoli. Rosé is made from Hondarrabi Beltza, often with Hondarrabi Zuri, by a short skin contact or by pressing the black grapes with the white.

law.classification: Three DOs share the name txakolina, the Basque word with its article, chacolí in Spanish, each named for a province. Getariako Txakolina was recognised by an order of 21 September 1989 for the communes of Getaria, Zarautz and Aia, and an order of 27 April 2007 extended it to the whole of Gipuzkoa. Bizkaiko Txakolina followed in 1994 for Bizkaia, and Arabako Txakolina in 2001 for the Ayala valley of Álava. The rules recommend Hondarrabi Zuri for white and Hondarrabi Beltza for red, and permit other grapes, among them Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Riesling and Chardonnay, and Folle Blanche in Bizkaia, only within a capped share of a winery's vineyard. The wines are white above all, with some rosé and a little red. Rioja Alavesa, in the south of Álava, belongs to the Rioja DOCa, not to txakoli.
tiers: Getariako Txakolina DO
1989, Gipuzkoa: first the communes of Getaria, Zarautz and Aia, extended to the whole province in 2007; the coastal heart of the style.
Bizkaiko Txakolina DO
1994, Bizkaia: vineyards scattered across the province, on the coast around Bakio and in the valleys inland.
Arabako Txakolina DO
2001, Álava: the Ayala valley, inland south of Bilbao, the last of the three.
Rioja DOCa (Rioja Alavesa)
The south of Álava belongs to Rioja, not to txakoli; the Rioja article holds it.
labels: Txakoli in Basque with its article; chacolí in Spanish.
The white and the black grape; zuri means white and beltza black.
Of Getaria, of Bizkaia, of Álava: the three DOs.
Rosé, from Hondarrabi Beltza with Hondarrabi Zuri.
To pour from a height, as txakoli is served in Basque bars.

places.name: Getaria
places.note: The fishing town on the Gipuzkoa coast west of San Sebastián that names the first txakoli DO; its vineyards climb the slopes above the town and the sea.

places.name: Zarautz
places.note: The beach town beside Getaria, one of the three communes of the DO in 1989, with vineyards on the hills behind it.

places.name: Aia
places.note: The hill commune inland of Getaria and Zarautz, the third of the original communes, with vineyards set back from the sea.

places.name: Bizkaia
places.note: The province of Bilbao, whose DO, Bizkaiko Txakolina, gathers vineyards scattered across the province, on the coast and in the valleys inland.

places.name: Bakio
places.note: A coastal town north of Bilbao, a historic centre of Bizkaia's txakoli, with vineyards on slopes facing the sea.

places.name: Ayala valley
places.note: The valley of the Nervión in northern Álava, around Amurrio, Llodio, Okondo, Artziniega and Ayala itself, sheltered by the Sierra Salvada but on the Atlantic side: the zone of Arabako Txakolina, with riper, less salty wines.

places.name: Rioja Alavesa
places.note: The south of Álava, beyond the Sierra de Cantabria, belongs to the Rioja DOCa; its own article, Rioja, holds it.

places.name: Irouléguy
places.note: The wine of the French Basque Country, across the Pyrenees; its own article, South West France, holds it.

producers.name: Ameztoi
producers.why: A Getaria family house with vineyards above the sea, known for its white and for a rosé of Hondarrabi Beltza.

producers.name: Talai Berri
producers.why: A family house in Zarautz, one of the original communes of the Getariako Txakolina DO.

producers.name: Itsasmendi
producers.why: A Bizkaiko Txakolina house near Gernika, known for whites of Hondarrabi Zuri, some kept on their lees.

producers.name: Doniene Gorrondona
producers.why: A Bakio estate, a reference for Bizkaia's txakoli, including a rare red of Hondarrabi Beltza.

producers.name: Señorío de Astobiza
producers.why: An Okondo estate in the Ayala valley, a reference for Arabako Txakolina.

exam: Place the País Vasco on the Atlantic coast of northern Spain, on the Bay of Biscay, with a moderate maritime climate: Green Spain.
Name the three DOs and their provinces: Getariako Txakolina (Gipuzkoa), Bizkaiko Txakolina (Bizkaia), Arabako Txakolina (Álava).
Know Getariako Txakolina as the first, recognised in 1989, and Arabako as the last, in 2001.
Know Hondarrabi Zuri as the white grape and Hondarrabi Beltza as the black.
Describe the style: chiefly dry white, lightly effervescent, high in acid, low in alcohol, meant for early drinking; reds and rosés are rare.
Know the winemaking: modern, temperature-controlled stainless steel tanks.
Pair it with oily seafood: anchovies, sardines and the pintxos of the coast.
Zarautz, Aia and Bakio, and the 2007 extension of Getaria's zone, are asked from Premier Cru; Folle Blanche as Mune Mahatsa from Grand Cru.
traps: Txakoli is Basque and Spanish; Vinho Verde is its Portuguese cousin, another country and other grapes.
The Basque Country holds Rioja Alavesa too; txakoli is the wine of the coast and the Ayala valley, not of Rioja.
Irouléguy is the French Basque wine, across the border, not a txakoli DO.
Zuri is white and beltza black: Hondarrabi Zuri for the whites, Hondarrabi Beltza for reds and rosés.
The prickle is the fermentation's own carbon dioxide kept in the wine; plain txakoli is not a sparkling wine made by a second fermentation.
Txakoli, txakolina and chacolí are one wine in Basque and Spanish spellings.

cards.b: The sharp, pale, faintly sparkling white of the Spanish Basque Country, from the rainy hills above the Bay of Biscay; low in alcohol, high in acid, drunk young.

cards.f: Txakoli: the three DOs and their provinces
cards.b: Getariako Txakolina (Gipuzkoa, 1989), Bizkaiko Txakolina (Bizkaia, 1994), Arabako Txakolina (Álava, 2001).
Recognised in 1989 around the fishing town of Getaria on the Gipuzkoa coast, the first of the three; the coastal heart of the style.

cards.f: Txakoli's two grapes and their colours
cards.b: Hondarrabi Zuri, white, for nearly all txakoli; Hondarrabi Beltza, black, for the rare reds and the rosés. Zuri means white, beltza black.
Chiefly dry white, lightly effervescent, high in acid and low in alcohol, meant for early drinking; reds and rosés are rare.

cards.f: How txakoli is made and served
cards.b: Cool fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel, bottled young with a little carbon dioxide kept in; poured from a height into a tumbler, with anchovies and oily seafood.

cards.f: Arabako Txakolina: where and how it differs
cards.b: The Ayala valley in northern Álava, inland, sheltered by the Sierra Salvada but Atlantic: riper and less salty wines than the coast's.
The DO of 1989 covered Getaria, Zarautz and Aia; an order of 27 April 2007 extended it to the whole of Gipuzkoa.
Bakio, on the coast north of Bilbao, is a historic centre of Bizkaia's txakoli; the DO of 1994 gathers vineyards across the province.

cards.f: The permitted grapes beyond the two Hondarrabis
cards.b: In a capped share: Gros Manseng (Izkiriota), Petit Courbu (Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia), Riesling and Chardonnay; in Bizkaia also Folle Blanche (Mune Mahatsa) and Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.q: Which white grape is the base of nearly all txakoli?
questions.exp: Hondarrabi Zuri, zuri meaning white, makes nearly all txakoli. Treixadura leads Ribeiro, Garnacha Blanca grows in Catalonia and Aragón, and Albariño is the grape of Rías Baixas.

questions.q: Which of the three txakoli DOs was recognised first, in 1989?
questions.exp: Getariako Txakolina, on the Gipuzkoa coast, was recognised in 1989. Bizkaiko Txakolina followed in 1994 and Arabako Txakolina in 2001.

questions.q: In which province is Arabako Txakolina made?
questions.exp: Arabako means of Álava: the DO covers the Ayala valley in the north of the province. Gipuzkoa is Getaria's province and Bizkaia Bakio's; Navarra is a separate region with its own DO.

questions.q: Which climate marks the txakoli vineyards of the Basque coast?
questions.exp: The Basque coast is moderate maritime, the Green Spain of the Atlantic north, with rain in every month. Warm Mediterranean belongs to Murcia, continental to the Duero plateau.

questions.q: Which black grape gives txakoli's rare reds and its rosés?
questions.exp: Hondarrabi Beltza, beltza meaning black, makes the few reds alone and the rosés with Hondarrabi Zuri.

questions.q: With which food is txakoli traditionally served on the Basque coast?
questions.exp: Txakoli's sharp acid, low alcohol and light prickle cut through oily seafood such as anchovies and sardines. Lamb, blue cheese and venison need more weight or sweetness.

questions.q: Besides Getaria, which two communes made up the Getariako Txakolina DO in 1989?
questions.exp: The DO first covered Getaria, Zarautz and Aia; an order of 2007 extended it to the whole of Gipuzkoa.

questions.q: Under which Basque name do the Bizkaiko Txakolina rules permit Folle Blanche?
questions.exp: Mune Mahatsa is Folle Blanche, allowed in a capped share in Bizkaia. Izkiriota is Gros Manseng, Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia Petit Courbu, and Hondarrabi Beltza the black grape.

regions.name: Ribeiro, Ribeira Sacra and Valdeorras
regions.summary: Inland Galicia, where the Atlantic loosens its grip along the Miño and the Sil. Four DOs share it. Ribeiro, around Ribadavia, was Galicia's historic export white and is built on Treixadura; Ribeira Sacra terraces Mencía on the steep walls of the Sil and Miño canyons; Valdeorras, the eastern gate on the Sil beside Bierzo, is the home of Godello, rescued from near loss from the 1970s; and Monterrei, on the Portuguese border, is the warmer, drier valley of the Támega. Soils run from granite to slate, the climate from Atlantic towards continental, and the wines from crisp whites to light, fragrant reds.

terroir.climate: Maritime on the coast, becoming more continental inland, and these valleys are the transition. Rain still comes off the Atlantic, but less of it than on the coast, and summers are warmer: the Miño valley around Ourense is hot in July and August. Ribeiro, sheltered from the sea by hills, is warmer than Rías Baixas, with its rain in winter and spring. Ribeira Sacra's canyons trap heat on their south-facing walls while the high ground above stays cool. Valdeorras, further east, has colder winters and more sun. Monterrei, in a rain shadow near Portugal, is warmer and drier than the other Galician DOs, with frost a spring risk. The warmth inland lets reds ripen, which the coast rarely manages.
terroir.soils: Granite, the soil the Court names for Galicia, much of it weathered to a coarse sand, covers Ribeiro, the Miño side of Ribeira Sacra and much of Monterrei. Slate and schist take over to the east: on the Sil's terraces in Ribeira Sacra and on the slopes of Valdeorras, a slate country, where the stone gives Godello and Mencía a mineral, stony edge. River terraces of clay, sand and gravel lie on the valley floors in Valdeorras and Monterrei, and alluvium beside the rivers in Ribeiro.
terroir.topography: Ribeiro lies on low hillsides and terraces where the Avia and the Arnoia meet the Miño around Ribadavia. Ribeira Sacra is a land of canyons: the Sil and the Miño cut gorges hundreds of metres deep, and vines climb their walls on narrow stone terraces from the water's edge upwards. Valdeorras is the Sil valley from O Barco to A Rúa, ringed by mountains, its vines on slopes and river terraces. Monterrei is the flat valley floor of the Támega around Verín and the hillsides that rise from it.
terroir.water: The Sil comes west out of Bierzo through Valdeorras and cuts the canyon of Ribeira Sacra before it joins the Miño near Os Peares; the Miño then runs south-west through Ourense and Ribeiro and becomes the Portuguese border down to the sea. Dams have turned stretches of both rivers into reservoirs, which soften the canyon's extremes. Ribeiro's Avia and Arnoia join the Miño near Ribadavia, and Monterrei's Támega flows south into Portugal to meet the Douro.

grapes.name: Treixadura
grapes.styles: Ribeiro's main white, later ripening and broader than Albariño, with pear, apple and blossom; blended with Godello, Loureira, Albariño and Torrontés, and the same vine as Portugal's Trajadura.

grapes.name: Godello
grapes.styles: The white of Valdeorras, almost lost by the 1970s and revived: fresh from steel, or textured, stony and mineral after lees or barrel; grown across all four DOs.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.styles: The red of Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei: light to medium-bodied, floral and red-fruited, with bright acidity and a stony note from slate.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: Grown inland too: a partner in Ribeiro's blends and one of the whites the Court names for Ribeira Sacra.

grapes.name: Loureira
grapes.styles: Loureiro in Portugal: an aromatic, laurel-scented white blended with Treixadura in Ribeiro.

grapes.name: Torrontés (Galicia)
grapes.styles: A Ribeiro white, a different vine from the Torrontés of Argentina, fresh and light in blends.

grapes.name: Merenzao
grapes.styles: The Trousseau of the Jura and Bastardo of Portugal: a pale, perfumed red of Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei.

grapes.name: Brancellao
grapes.styles: A pale, fragrant old red of Ribeira Sacra and Ribeiro, blended with Mencía or bottled alone by a few houses.

grapes.name: Sousón
grapes.styles: A dark, sharp red that brings colour and acidity to blends in Ribeiro and Ribeira Sacra.

grapes.name: Doña Blanca
grapes.styles: Dona Branca in Galician, a soft white of Valdeorras and Monterrei, often blended with Godello.

grapes.name: Garnacha Tintorera
grapes.styles: The red-fleshed Alicante Bouschet, grown in Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra for colour.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.styles: Planted for volume in the last century, especially in Valdeorras, and now giving way to Godello.

wines.note: Dry, with pear, stone fruit, fennel and a stony, saline finish; fresh from steel or rounder after lees or barrel. Serve it with roast fish, scallops, octopus and white meats.
Light to medium-bodied, with violet, raspberry, red cherry and slate, bright acidity and fine tannin. Serve it slightly cool with charcuterie, empanada or roast pork.
A blend led by Treixadura with Godello, Loureira, Albariño or Torrontés: fresh, floral and fruity, rounder than a coastal Albariño; for seafood, empanada and the soft cheeses of Galicia.
Riper and fuller than the coast's whites, from Godello, Treixadura and Dona Branca in the warm Támega valley; for grilled fish and white meats.
A naturally sweet wine from raisined grapes, amber, honeyed and nutty with fresh acidity; a rare bottle for desserts and blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Ribeira Sacra's vineyards hang on terraces of dry stone built into canyon walls so steep that the work is all by hand: grapes come up in baskets on the shoulder or on small rack railways that climb the slope, and some riverside plots were once reached by boat. The trade calls it heroic viticulture, and terraces here may go back to Roman times. Elsewhere the slopes are gentler and most vines are trained on wires. Atlantic rain brings mildew and rot in wet years, so canopy work and the timing of the harvest matter; spring frost is the threat in Monterrei and Valdeorras. After phylloxera much of the vineyard was replanted with Palomino and Garnacha Tintorera for volume. In Valdeorras a revival project known as ReViVal, begun in 1974, gathered the last old Godello vines and propagated them, and the native grapes have been returning across the four DOs since. Holdings are small and often part time, and steep plots are abandoned when no one is left to work them.
made.winemaking: Whites are made in steel at cool temperatures for freshness, and Godello is often kept on its lees, and some is fermented and aged in barrel or larger wood for texture, much as white Burgundy is. Ribeiro blends several grapes with Treixadura at the centre. Mencía is handled gently: short, cool macerations, sometimes with whole bunches, and ageing in steel or in used barrels and larger casks, so that the perfume and the stony note stay in front; most Ribeira Sacra reds are bottled young, with barrel-aged wines above them. Ribeiro's Tostado is made from grapes dried after picking until they are raisined, then pressed and slowly fermented into a naturally sweet wine. Since 2025 Ribeiro's rules also allow a quality sparkling wine made by the traditional method from the native grapes, Brut or Brut Nature.

law.classification: Four DOs share inland Galicia. Ribeiro was recognised under the Estatuto del Vino of 1932, among Spain's earliest denominations, and Valdeorras, from the middle of the century, was the second in Galicia; Monterrei became a full DO in 1994 and Ribeira Sacra in 1996. Each sets out preferred native grapes and authorised others. Ribeira Sacra has five subzones along its two rivers in Lugo and Ourense provinces: Amandi, Chantada, Quiroga-Bibei, Ribeiras do Miño and Ribeiras do Sil. Monterrei has two, Val de Monterrei and Ladeira de Monterrei. Ribeiro's rules, amended in 2025, set the still wines of the preferred native grapes apart from those of secondary grapes and add a traditional-method sparkling wine; Ribeira Sacra's, also amended in 2025, lower the maximum yield allowed for black grapes. The national ageing terms apply. Bierzo, beside Valdeorras, lies in Castilla y León and has its own article.
tiers: Ribeiro DO
1932, under the Estatuto del Vino: the Miño, Avia and Arnoia valleys around Ribadavia; whites led by Treixadura, reds, Tostado and, since 2025, traditional-method sparkling.
Valdeorras DO
The Sil valley in eastern Ourense, Galicia's second DO after Ribeiro: Godello whites and Mencía reds.
Ribeira Sacra DO
1996: the canyons of the Sil and Miño in Lugo and Ourense, five subzones; Mencía reds above all, with Godello and Albariño whites.
Monterrei DO
1994: the Támega valley at Verín on the Portuguese border, two subzones; Godello, Treixadura and Dona Branca whites, Mencía and Merenzao reds.
labels: The red grape of Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei.
Ribeiro's naturally sweet wine from raisined grapes.
A Ribeira Sacra subzone on the Sil, a name often seen on labels.
Wine, vintage and winery in Galician.

places.name: Ribeiro
places.note: The valleys of the Miño, Avia and Arnoia around Ribadavia in Ourense province, Galicia's historic export white: Treixadura-led blends, reds of native grapes and the sweet Tostado.

places.name: Ribadavia
places.note: The old town where the Avia meets the Miño, with its medieval quarter, long the trading heart of Ribeiro's wine, which was shipped to England and northern Europe in the late Middle Ages.

places.name: Ribeira Sacra
places.note: The canyons of the Sil and the Miño in Lugo and Ourense provinces, terraced by hand and named for the monasteries along the rivers; Mencía reds, Godello and Albariño whites.

places.name: Amandi
places.note: On the Sil's north bank in Lugo province, south-facing terraces of slate that give ripe, deep Mencía; a name often seen on labels.

places.name: Chantada
places.note: The Miño around the town of Chantada, on granite, with gentler and cooler slopes than the Sil's.

places.name: Quiroga-Bibei
places.note: The eastern subzone, on the Sil and its tributary the Bibei towards Valdeorras, warmer and drier than the rest.

places.name: Ribeiras do Miño
places.note: The terraced banks of the Miño downstream towards its meeting with the Sil.

places.name: Ribeiras do Sil
places.note: The Sil's southern bank in Ourense province, across the canyon from Amandi, with cooler, mostly north-facing terraces.

places.name: Valdeorras
places.note: The Sil valley in eastern Ourense around O Barco and A Rúa, beside Bierzo, on slate, granite and river terraces: the home of Godello, with Mencía reds.

places.name: O Barco de Valdeorras
places.note: The main town of the valley, on the Sil near the border with Bierzo.

places.name: Monterrei
places.note: The Támega valley around Verín against the Portuguese border, in a rain shadow, warmer and drier than the rest of Galicia, with two subzones, Val de Monterrei and Ladeira de Monterrei.

places.name: Verín
places.note: The town at the heart of the valley, below the castle of Monterrei that gives the DO its name.

places.name: Bierzo
places.note: Upstream on the Sil in Castilla y León, sharing Mencía, Godello and slate; its own article, Bierzo, holds it.

producers.name: Godeval
producers.why: A Valdeorras house founded in the 1980s by people of the Godello revival, an early bottler of Godello alone.

producers.name: Valdesil
producers.why: A family estate of Valdeorras with very old Godello vines on slate.

producers.name: Bodegas A Tapada
producers.why: A Valdeorras estate whose Guitián Godello, kept on its lees or fermented in barrel, helped make the grape's name.

producers.name: Regina Viarum
producers.why: An Amandi estate on the Sil's slate terraces, known for Mencía.

producers.name: Algueira
producers.why: An Amandi estate known for Mencía, Merenzao and Brancellao from terraces above the Sil.

producers.name: Dominio do Bibei
producers.why: An estate of the Bibei valley in Quiroga-Bibei, known for Mencía-based reds and Godello.

producers.name: Viña Costeira
producers.why: The trading name of Ribeiro's co-operative at Ribadavia, a widely seen Treixadura-led Ribeiro.

producers.name: Coto de Gomariz
producers.why: An estate of the Avia valley in Ribeiro, a reference for Treixadura-led whites and native reds.

producers.name: Quinta da Muradella
producers.why: A Verín estate that revived old native grapes of the Támega valley.

exam: Place inland Galicia: the Miño and Sil valleys in Ourense and Lugo provinces, maritime on the coast becoming more continental inland.
Know Valdeorras: Godello whites and Mencía reds, on slate and granite; Godello rescued from near loss from the 1970s.
Know Ribeira Sacra: steep, terraced vineyards on the canyons of the Sil and Miño; whites Albariño and Godello, red Mencía.
Give granite as the soil the Court names for Galicia, and add slate for Valdeorras and the Sil's terraces.
Know the styles: dry, crisp whites and light reds; fresh and neutral Godello in Valdeorras; Mencía, Godello and Albariño in Ribeira Sacra.
Know the winemaking: steel for freshness, lees for Godello's texture and occasional barrique, barrica in Spanish.
Know Ribeiro as the historic export white built on Treixadura, and Monterrei as the warmer, drier valley on the Portuguese border.
Ribeira Sacra's five subzones and Ribeiro's 2025 sparkling wine are asked from Premier Cru; Ribeiro's medieval trade with England and the Tostado from Grand Cru.
traps: Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra are Galician DOs; Bierzo, upstream on the same river, is in Castilla y León.
Ribeiro and Ribeira Sacra are different DOs: Ribeiro is the white-led valley around Ribadavia, Ribeira Sacra the terraced canyons and their Mencía.
Godello is not Albariño: broader, stonier and less aromatic; Valdeorras is its home, Rías Baixas Albariño's.
Mencía here is light and floral, not a dark, heavy red.
Treixadura is Portugal's Trajadura and Loureira is Loureiro, the same vines across the Miño.
Galician Torrontés is a different vine from the Torrontés of Argentina.
Merenzao is Trousseau, the Jura's red, called Bastardo in Portugal.

cards.b: Godello whites and Mencía reds from the Sil valley in eastern Ourense, on slate, granite and river terraces; Galicia's eastern gate, beside Bierzo.

cards.f: Ribeira Sacra: the land and the grapes
cards.b: Steep stone terraces on the canyons of the Sil and Miño, worked by hand; Mencía reds, with Godello and Albariño whites.
The Miño, Avia and Arnoia valleys around Ribadavia: Treixadura-led white blends, Galicia's historic export wine; a DO under the Estatuto del Vino of 1932.

cards.f: Monterrei: where and how it differs
cards.b: The Támega valley at Verín on the Portuguese border, in a rain shadow: warmer and drier than the rest of Galicia; Godello, Treixadura, Mencía.
Almost lost by the 1970s; the ReViVal project in Valdeorras, begun in 1974, gathered the last old vines and propagated them. Now the badge of Valdeorras.
The Sil flows west from Bierzo through Valdeorras and cuts Ribeira Sacra's canyon, then joins the Miño, which runs through Ourense and Ribeiro to Portugal.

cards.f: Mencía in Ribeira Sacra: the style
cards.b: Light to medium-bodied, violet, raspberry and slate, bright acid and fine tannin; served slightly cool, mostly bottled young.
Amandi, Chantada, Quiroga-Bibei, Ribeiras do Miño and Ribeiras do Sil, along the two rivers in Lugo and Ourense; Ribeira Sacra became a DO in 1996.
Still wines of the preferred native grapes set apart from those of secondary grapes, and a quality sparkling wine by the traditional method from native grapes, Brut or Brut Nature.

cards.f: Tostado do Ribeiro: what and how
cards.b: Ribeiro's naturally sweet wine: grapes dried after picking until raisined, then pressed and slowly fermented; amber, honeyed and nutty.

questions.q: Which white grape is the signature of Valdeorras?
questions.exp: Godello, revived from near loss in the 1970s, is the white of Valdeorras. Albariño belongs to Rías Baixas, Treixadura to Ribeiro and Verdejo to Rueda.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the wines of Ribeira Sacra?
questions.exp: Mencía makes Ribeira Sacra's light, floral reds on the canyon terraces. Tempranillo leads Rioja and the Duero, Garnacha Navarra and Priorat, and Monastrell Jumilla.

questions.q: Which white grape is at the centre of Ribeiro's blends?
questions.exp: Treixadura, later ripening and broader than Albariño, leads Ribeiro's whites with Godello, Loureira, Albariño and Torrontés. In Portugal the same vine is Trajadura.

questions.q: Which river, flowing west out of Bierzo, cuts the canyon of Ribeira Sacra?
questions.exp: The Sil passes through Valdeorras and cuts Ribeira Sacra's canyon before joining the Miño. The Duero drains Ribera and Toro, the Ebro Rioja, and the Tajo central Spain.

questions.q: Which Galician DO lies in the Támega valley against the Portuguese border?
questions.exp: Monterrei surrounds Verín in the Támega valley, warmer and drier than the rest of Galicia. Ribeiro lies on the Miño around Ribadavia, Ribeira Sacra in the canyons and Valdeorras on the Sil.

questions.q: Which soil, beside granite, marks the slopes of Valdeorras?
questions.exp: Valdeorras is slate country, and the stone gives Godello and Mencía a mineral edge. Limestone marks the Côte d'Or, albariza Jerez and volcanic ash the Canary Islands.

questions.q: Which Ribeira Sacra subzone, in Lugo province on the Sil, is known for south-facing terraces of slate?
questions.exp: Amandi's slate terraces on the Sil's north bank face south and give ripe, deep Mencía. The other subzones are Chantada, Quiroga-Bibei, Ribeiras do Miño and Ribeiras do Sil.

questions.q: What is Ribeiro's naturally sweet wine from raisined grapes called?
questions.exp: Tostado is made from grapes dried after picking until raisined, then pressed and slowly fermented into an amber, honeyed sweet wine.
